title: Tired, Cold and Slow, with Angina / Start Low, Go Slow

blocks.text: Tired, Cold and Slow, with Angina / Start Low, Go Slow

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-30 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) · 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min · Guidelines: NICE NG145 Thyroid disease: assessment and management (published 20 November 2019; last updated 12 October 2023) · Related AMaC: None identified

Dear Doctor, a 74-year-old retired seamstress. Six months of tiredness, feeling cold, weight gain and constipation. Her GP found a high TSH and a low free T4 on two occasions. She has stable angina. Please assess and advise.
Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Tiredness and cold intolerance with a high TSH and low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism; the lesson is to start levothyroxine low and slow in an older woman with angina, and to monitor TSH.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates give the standard full dose by weight. Pass: start 25 to 50 micrograms with titration, check an ECG, and warn about chest pain. Fail: a full replacement dose in a woman with angina.

rows: Hypothyroid, and why? Get the story.
"Tell me about the tiredness, the cold, your weight and bowels. Any chest pain on effort?"
Introduce, consent, ask about pain; symptoms, angina, drugs, family, past thyroid treatment.
Look for signs and heart disease.
"May I feel your neck and pulse, check your reflexes and blood pressure?"
Pulse, BP, skin, hair, voice, goitre, ankle reflexes, oedema.
Treat safely in the older heart.
"I'd start a low dose of levothyroxine and build up slowly."
Dose, ECG, titration, TSH at set intervals, chest-pain warning.
Share the plan; find her worry.
Explain tablets, timing, monitoring, options; safety net; check understanding.
Rushes her or ignores that she is tired and cold
Introduces, consents, asks about discomfort, keeps her warm and covered
Offers a chaperone, a seat and a blanket, and thanks her for coming
Does not ask about chest pain or drugs
Asks symptoms, angina pattern, drugs, past thyroid problems, family history and mood
Also asks about amiodarone, lithium, previous radioiodine, biotin and calcium or iron tablets
Acknowledges worry; asks what concerns her
Finds the fear that her forgetfulness is dementia, and answers honestly
Reports a goitre or exophthalmos that is absent
Pulse 54 regular, BP 148/88, dry skin, slow-relaxing ankle reflexes, no goitre (scenario)
Adds hair, voice and periorbital puffiness, carpal tunnel signs, and states negatives: no oedema, no heart failure
Primary hypothyroidism, likely autoimmune, with other causes and drug causes considered
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): starts a full replacement dose
Starts 25 to 50 micrograms daily and titrates; ECG; TSH every 3 months until stable, then yearly
Cites NICE NG145; explains timing on an empty stomach, spacing from iron and calcium, and that TSH may take months to settle
Benefits, risks and alternatives; chest-pain warning; checks understanding
Covers lifelong treatment, doing nothing, how a dose rise could bring angina and when to return

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are. A 74-year-old retired seamstress. Gentle, a bit slow, worried. Widowed, lives alone, daughter nearby.
Opening line. "I'm always cold and tired. The doctor says my thyroid is underactive."
Volunteered. Tired and cold for six months; weight gain; constipation.

Only if asked. Dry skin and hair. Chest tightness on walking uphill, relieved by rest and a GTN spray; no rest pain. Forgetfulness. No thyroid surgery or radioiodine. No lithium or amiodarone. Takes aspirin, a statin and a calcium tablet daily, and uses GTN spray when needed. No allergies. Never smoked. A sherry at Christmas. No recent travel. Your mother had an underactive thyroid and your sister has dementia. You do not drive.
Hidden concern. You fear your forgetfulness means dementia like your sister. Reveal only if asked what worries you most.
Your questions. "Will the tablets cure it?" "Is it safe for my heart?" "How long will I take them?" "Will I stop feeling forgetful?"
How you react. Good handling: you agree to start low and have the tests. Poor handling: if told to start the full dose you say you will take it and ask no questions.

Findings (released as each step is done). Slow, dry skin, thin hair. Pulse 54 regular; BP 148/88 (scenario values). No goitre. Ankle reflexes slow to relax. No oedema. Chest clear; heart sounds normal. Weight 68 kg (scenario). TSH raised and free T4 low on two samples; ECG sinus bradycardia, no ischaemic change (scenario).

Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis (R5): primary hypothyroidism. Q2 Dose (R6): NICE NG145 advises considering 25 to 50 micrograms daily with titration for adults aged 65 and over or with cardiovascular disease; 1.6 micrograms per kilogram for others. Q3 Monitoring (R6): TSH every 3 months until stable, then yearly; it may take up to 6 months to settle. Q4 Risk (R6): levothyroxine can provoke angina. Q5 Advice (R7): timing and spacing of tablets.
Curveball 1. "She has chest pain at rest after the first dose." (R6) Safe: stop the dose rise; urgent assessment; ECG.
Curveball 2. "The TSH is raised but free T4 is normal." (R5) Safe: subclinical hypothyroidism; repeat and discuss.
Curveball 3. "She is drowsy, hypothermic and confused." (R5) Safe: myxoedema coma; emergency care.
Curveball 4. "Her daughter wants her to take the full dose." (R7) Safe: explain why slow titration is safer.
Introduces, consents and keeps her warm (G)
Asks symptoms and angina pattern (C)
Asks drugs, thyroid history and family history (C)
Acknowledges her view and asks what worries her (F)
Examines pulse, blood pressure and reflexes (A)
Examines neck for goitre (A)
Reports slow pulse, dry skin and slow reflexes (B)
Names primary hypothyroidism (D)
Starts a low dose and plans an ECG (E)
Plans TSH monitoring and a chest-pain warning (E)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Sit down. [R1 Fail] (No angina or drug history. [R2 Fail] [R3 Fail])
(Reports a goitre that is not there. [R4 Fail])
CANDIDATE: It's your age. [R5 Fail] Start 100 micrograms. [R6 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Come back next year. [R7 Fail]

Examiner note: No history, a wrong diagnosis and an unsafe dose. A full replacement dose in a woman with angina can provoke chest pain and is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail).
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello, I'm one of the doctors. May I feel your neck and pulse and check your reflexes? Tell me if anything is uncomfortable. I'll keep you warm and covered. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Tell me about the tiredness and cold. Any chest tightness on effort? Which tablets do you take? Any thyroid treatment before, or thyroid problems in the family? How is your mood? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Chest tightness uphill. I'm afraid it's dementia.
CANDIDATE: That's a real worry. What concerns you most? [R3 Pass]
(Checks pulse, BP, skin, neck and reflexes; finds slow pulse, dry skin, slow reflexes and no goitre. [R4 Pass])
CANDIDATE: This is primary hypothyroidism. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I'd start 25 to 50 micrograms of levothyroxine and build up slowly, check an ECG, and check TSH every 3 months until stable, then yearly. [R6 Pass]

CANDIDATE: The tablets replace the hormone you lack and should ease the tiredness. Too fast a rise can bring on angina, so we go slowly; the alternative is to wait, which prolongs your symptoms. Report chest pain at once. Can you tell me what you will do if you get it? [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and clear. Did not cite NICE or address the fear of dementia fully.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? I'll keep you warm and covered. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any amiodarone, lithium, radioiodine, biotin, iron or calcium tablets? [R2 High]
PATIENT: I'm afraid I'm getting dementia.
CANDIDATE: Thank you for telling me. An underactive thyroid can slow thinking, and it often improves with treatment. [R3 High]
(Also checks hair, voice, periorbital puffiness and carpal tunnel signs; no oedema or heart failure. [R4 High])
CANDIDATE: Primary hypothyroidism, likely autoimmune; drugs and other causes considered. [R5 High]

CANDIDATE: NICE NG145 advises starting 25 to 50 micrograms for people over 65 or with heart disease; take it on an empty stomach, spaced from iron and calcium; TSH may take up to 6 months to settle. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: Options: start now, or wait, which prolongs symptoms. Treatment is lifelong; a dose rise can bring angina, so report chest pain. [R7 High]
Examiner note: Answered the fear and explained dose, spacing and monitoring.
R6: A full replacement dose in a woman with angina is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): it can provoke chest pain.
R2: Not asking about angina and drugs misses the cardiac risk.
R4: Reporting a goitre not present shows signs were assumed.
R5: Blaming age ignores the abnormal thyroid tests.
R7: Instructions without options leave her without a say.
"Do you get chest tightness on effort?"
"I'd start low and build up slowly."
"What worries you most?"

NICE NG145 (published 20 November 2019; last updated 12 October 2023): consider 1.6 micrograms per kilogram daily in adults under 65 without cardiovascular disease; consider 25 to 50 micrograms daily with titration for adults aged 65 and over or with cardiovascular disease; aim for TSH in the reference range; consider TSH every 3 months until stable, then yearly; it can take up to 6 months to settle after a very high starting level.
THINK: Hypothyroid; angina.
SAY: "I'd start low and go slow, check an ECG and your TSH."
DO: Pulse; BP; reflexes; neck; ECG.
NUMBERS: 25 to 50 micrograms; TSH every 3 months (NICE NG145).
TRAP: Full dose in angina.
FINISH: Report chest pain; TSH in 3 months.
